title: What a misl was
hookLine: a misl was a band of equals with its own chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa

lines: EACH BAND WITH ITS OWN CHIEF.
cards: A rider comes into Amritsar with a few dozen horsemen behind him. Another arrives from the north with his own men, and another from across the river. None of them is king of the others.
Each band has its own chief, its own villages, its own way of doing things. But when they reach the Guru's city, they sit down together as one Khalsa.
For the next part of this path, those bands are the story, and the name for the band itself is today's word: misl.

teach.h: A BAND AROUND A CHIEF, THE SARDAR.
teach.b: Four turns. First, a misl was a band. Tradition says it gathered around a chief, a sardar, who had earned the trust of the riders with him.
It held land and protected the villages under it, and those villages paid it for that protection. Second, a band of equals. In the way Sikh histories tell it, a rider wasn't the chief's servant.

teach.h: RIDERS WHO CHOSE TO RIDE WITH HIM.
teach.b: He was a Singh of the Khalsa who had chosen to ride with this sardar, and tradition says he could leave and ride with another. What was won was shared out. The chief led people who stood on the same ground he did.
Third, the misls didn't stand alone.

teach.h: JOINED TOGETHER IN THE DAL KHALSA.
teach.b: Together they made up the Dal Khalsa, the army of the Khalsa, and when a danger was too big for one band, they rode as one.

Tradition says that at the great gatherings in Amritsar, the Sarbat Khalsa, the chiefs met before the Guru Granth Sahib and agreed on a gurmata, a resolution in the Guru's presence, which bound every band.

teach.h: BORN OUT OF THE HARD CENTURY.
teach.b: Fourth, the misls were what the hard century produced. Small bands that had hidden in forests and deserts now held the countryside.
Over the coming days, the path visits them one by one: who led them, where they rode, what each became. Some grew strong. Some stayed small.
One would one day give rise to a kingdom.
But they started in the same place: a band of equals.

how: Sikhs learn about the misls in Sikh histories and at gurdwara talks, and the gurmata, a decision made together in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, is still part of how the Panth gathers.

o: fight it alone to keep your band's honor.

give up your land and ride away.
games.why: tradition says the chiefs met before the Guru Granth Sahib, agreed a gurmata, and rode together as the Dal Khalsa.

practice: Bring to mind a group where no one was above anyone else: a kitchen crew, a study group, a few friends moving a couch up three flights of stairs.
Notice who led, and how, and what made it feel equal, letting each face come up for a breath. If you pray, say Waheguru softly as each face comes.

wordCard.voice: Misl. A Sikh band with its own chief, its riders free to join it, joined to the other bands in the Dal Khalsa. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for misl, a band of the Khalsa with its own chief.
